Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news has an apocalyptic streak, a good deal of painters' private lives, and a few small things close to home.

Let me begin with the end of the world, which seems to be this week's theme. Tomorrow, the eighteenth of November, at half past two in the afternoon, the Musée de Grenoble hosts a talk in its Au fil du Texte series on the Apocalypse of Angers. It connects that great medieval tapestry cycle to its literary source, the Book of Revelation, so it is a chance to see how a text becomes image, thread by thread. And The Guardian has an exclusive on a rare sixteenth-century Book of Miracles, a set of one hundred and sixty-seven paintings of apocalyptic omens and extreme weather. It may fetch around one million pounds at auction, with public institutions given the first chance to bid. The paper quotes a description of it as the sixteenth-century version of doomscrolling, which rather makes one see the pages differently: comets, storms and portents, gathered by people who couldn't stop looking.

Staying close to home, the Musée de Grenoble has other things going on around its exhibition Libérer la couleur. The museum's library has put together a selection of books on Anne Truitt, for anyone wanting to go further than the gallery walls allow. Yesterday afternoon, the Friends of the Museum also held a session built around Martin Provost's 2023 film on Pierre Bonnard and Marthe, a painter's life told as drama. If you missed it, the film is worth looking out for. On the local news side, Ici-Grenoble reports on an encounter with Mathilde Gal around the exhibition Des vies orageuses. The text is short, so I wouldn't promise much detail, but it carries the artist's own words. And from L'Impartial de la Drôme comes a piece on a painting from Romans-sur-Isère, described as a witness to a vanished Isère. It's a small story, but exactly the kind where a picture does the work of a history essay.

Now, painters and the people around them. The Guardian has a lively piece on a new Edward Hopper biography, which suggests that his marriage to Josephine Nivison Hopper, and the troubles in their bedroom, surfaced in his famous melancholy paintings. Whether one wants to read those lonely rooms as autobiography is of course another matter, but it's a good prompt for a class on how much a biography should be allowed to tell us about a text or a canvas. Hyperallergic, meanwhile, reviews James Cahill's book on David Hockney and his Beverly Hills patron, which looks at the relationship between a painter and the person who made some of his work possible. The same piece wanders off into arts journalism and a Congressional bill, which you can happily skip.

For something older and quieter, the National Gallery has released a video on how Jan van Eyck transformed portraiture in the fifteenth century. Curators from London and Bruges talk about his realism and the hidden visual clues in his work. It's the sort of video that rewards a second look at a painting, rather like rereading a novel and noticing what the narrator let slip. And if you'd like a quick introduction to someone you may not know well, Beaux Arts Magazine offers Théo Van Rysselberghe in three minutes. He was a Belgian neo-impressionist painter, described as an anarchist, with a considerable international reach.

Now a few exhibitions further afield, all of them from the French press, so possibly worth a weekend trip. Dedicated to André Derain, the show called L'art est un jeu looks at the painter whose bold colour helped launch Fauvism. The coverage is thin, but his friendships and rivalries with his contemporaries are a story in themselves. Colour comes up again in Sculpter la couleur, which brings masterpieces from the Museo Nacional de Escultura in Valladolid, and focuses on painted sculpture. It explores how colour gave Spanish religious figures their life, which sounds vivid, and rather theatrical. At the Musée d'arts de Nantes, an exhibition on women and surrealism brings to light women artists long overshadowed by their male peers. It invites a natural link to surrealist writing, and perhaps a reading list. And in the south, Château La Coste is showing recent sculpture by Yoshitomo Nara, whose work often has a childlike and melancholy edge, and a strong emotional voice.

Finally, a bit of photography. The Guardian reviews the twenty-ninth Paris Photo, held at the Grand Palais during France's bicentenary of photography. The critic asks which images actually offered new ways of seeing, and the headline promises failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film. It's an entertaining read, and a reminder of how young the medium still is.

That's everything for this morning, Yamuna, so I hope the day gives you a little time to look at something slowly.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news has a pleasingly literary shape: an apocalypse in tapestry, a painter's marriage read like a novel, and a good handful of exhibitions where colour does most of the talking.

Let me begin close to home, at the Musée de Grenoble, where there is something for you tomorrow. On Wednesday the eighteenth of November, at half past two in the afternoon, the museum holds a talk in its Au fil du Texte series on the Apocalypse of Angers. This is the great medieval tapestry cycle, and the talk sets it beside its literary source, the Book of Revelation. I like the way the series is named, because it follows the thread of a text. Here the text is one of the strangest and most visual in all of scripture, and the tapestry turns its fevered images into something you can stand in front of. If you can slip away at that hour, it is the kind of session that gives a teacher fresh ways to talk about how a written vision becomes a picture.

Yesterday afternoon, also at half past two, the museum's Friends held a session centred on Martin Provost's 2023 film about Pierre Bonnard and Marthe. It has already taken place, so I mention it mainly in case you hear it discussed. Bonnard's life with Marthe is the sort of story that painters' biographies love, and a film that treats it as drama sits well beside the museum's current attention to colour.

That current attention leads to the museum library, which has put together a selection of books on Anne Truitt to accompany the exhibition "Libérer la couleur". It is useful for anyone who wants to go beyond the walls of the show. A library selection like this is a quiet pleasure. You can read around an artist at your own pace, and the exhibition becomes a conversation rather than a single visit. If you are planning to see the show, a look at the shelves first or afterwards could give you a way into Truitt's work.

Still in Grenoble, Ici-Grenoble reports on an encounter with Mathilde Gal around the exhibition "Des vies orageuses", which can be translated as "stormy lives". The piece is brief, so it is worth a look mainly for the exhibition itself and for the artist's own words. A title like that promises narrative, and I rather suspect it would appeal to the part of you that likes characters with turbulent inner weather.

The last local item comes from a little further down the river. L'Impartial de la Drôme has a piece from Romans-sur-Isère about a painting that serves as a witness to a vanished Isère. I like this idea very much. A landscape or a scene painted in one generation becomes, in the next, a document of something that no longer exists, and so a painting can teach history in the way you value in the best historical novels. The Isère it shows has gone, but the canvas remembers it.

That brings me to apocalypse again, because The Guardian has an exclusive that rhymes beautifully with tomorrow's talk in Grenoble. It concerns a rare sixteenth-century work known as the Book of Miracles, a set of one hundred and sixty-seven paintings of apocalyptic omens and extreme weather. It may fetch around one million pounds at auction, and public institutions have the first chance to bid. The headline gives the best line, with one voice calling it "the sixteenth-century version of doomscrolling". The comparison is vivid because it is apt. Here is a society looking nervously at the sky, collecting portents, and finding that the images of disaster have a terrible fascination of their own. For a classroom, it might be a lovely bridge between the Book of Revelation, the medieval tapestry at Angers, and our own habit of reading bad news late at night. Whether the book ends up in a public collection is something we will have to wait and see.

Now to painters and the stories we tell about them, which is where several of today's pieces meet. The Guardian also has a piece on a new biography of Edward Hopper, under the headline "His wife was horrified". The book suggests that his marriage to Josephine Nivison Hopper, and the troubles in their bedroom, surfaced in famous works, including those melancholy paintings we all know. It is a strong piece on a question that every teacher of literature will recognise: how far can we read a creator's private life into the work? Hopper's canvases are famously quiet, full of people sitting apart in rooms and light. A biography that says the silence belongs to a marriage is a bold claim, and whether you find it persuasive or reductive, it makes for good discussion. It is the same debate we have about a novelist and their narrator.

Another painter and another relationship: Hyperallergic reviews James Cahill's book on David Hockney and his Beverly Hills patron. The relationship between artist and patron is one of the oldest stories in art, and it has its own tensions, between independence and dependence and between friendship and commission. I should warn you that the same piece also wanders into arts journalism and a Congressional bill, which are outside your interests, so you may want to read only the first part.

For a different sort of portrait, the National Gallery has published a video on how Jan van Eyck transformed portraiture in the fifteenth century. Curators from London and Bruges talk about his realism and the hidden visual clues in his paintings. I find the idea of hidden clues irresistible. A van Eyck portrait is almost a text to be decoded, and the curators help you read it closely, as you would read a poem. The video is on the National Gallery's YouTube channel, and it would make a handsome companion to any lesson on painting and writing.

If you want a quicker acquaintance with a painter you may not know well, Beaux Arts Magazine offers Théo Van Rysselberghe in three minutes. He was a Belgian painter of neo-impressionism, described as an anarchist, and the piece also touches on his international reach. Neo-impressionism is the movement of tiny dots and luminous colour, and an anarchist painting in that careful, patient manner is an appealing contradiction. It is short and accessible, ideal for a coffee break.

Let me turn now to exhibitions elsewhere in France, where colour is the unifying theme. The journal jds.fr has three items. First, "André Derain. L'art est un jeu", devoted to the painter whose bold colour helped launch Fauvism. The text is thin, but Derain's links with his contemporaries make the exhibition a good fit for you, since the Fauves were a movement full of friendships, rivalries and shared experiments, rather like a literary circle.

Second, "Sculpter la couleur" presents masterpieces from the Museo Nacional de Escultura in Valladolid, focusing on painted sculpture. It explores how colour gave Spanish religious figures their life. I find this subject very vivid. We tend to imagine sculpture as pale stone or dark bronze, so the idea of figures painted to look almost breathing, in churches and processions, is a good reminder that colour was once part of how sacred stories were told. It connects, in its way, to the Apocalypse tapestry we began with: images made to be believed, and to move the viewer.

Third, the Musée d'arts de Nantes has an exhibition on women and surrealism, which brings to light women artists long overshadowed by their male peers. It also invites links to surrealist writing, which I know suits your taste. Surrealism was as much a literary movement as a visual one, and rediscovering the women who worked within it changes how one reads the whole story. It could be a fine source of fresh names for a syllabus.

Another voice with a strong emotional note comes from Arts in the City, which covers an exhibition of recent sculpture by Yoshitomo Nara at Château La Coste. Nara's work often has a childlike and melancholy edge, and that mixture of innocence and sadness gives it a very direct emotional voice, much like a narrator who seems to speak simply and says something unsettling.

Last, a lively read from The Guardian: a review of the twenty-ninth Paris Photo fair at the Grand Palais, held during France's bicentenary of photography. The review asks which images offered genuinely new ways of seeing. Its headline, "Quel head trip!", is followed by a promise of failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film, which tells you the writer had a good time. Two hundred years of photography is a long story, and the piece is a pleasure for anyone who likes to see how an old art keeps reinventing its eye.

That is the round for today, Yamuna. If tomorrow afternoon finds you in front of the Apocalypse, I hope the dragons are kind.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle day in the literary pages, with a good deal about writers' lives, old stories and the way history seeps into fiction.

Let me begin with Anita Brookner, who turns up twice. The New York Times reviews Hermione Lee's new biography, Anita Brookner: Art and Life, which it says corrects some of the public perceptions of the novelist's private life. The pairing of art and life in the title feels apt for a writer whose books, and whose career as an art historian, were so bound up with looking closely at pictures. Alongside it, Literary Hub has an essay on how Brookner restarted her life at fifty-two, beginning again as a novelist while still teaching. It's a heartening thing to read on a grey November morning: a whole second life, and a whole body of work, beginning at an age when many people assume the story is already written.

From there, a cluster of pieces about history and the old stories we keep returning to. Literary Hub offers an appreciative essay on Daphnis and Chloe, Longus's pastoral romance, which opens with a prayer that it will bring pleasure and comfort to lovers. The prose is described as lyrical and musical, so it may be one to dip into for the sound of the sentences alone. Literary Hub also has its weekly literary-history piece, this time on the Man in the Iron Mask, the prisoner arrested in sixteen sixty-nine during the reign of Louis the Fourteenth, whose identity was never revealed. A very French mystery, and one that has fed novelists for centuries. And in a more material vein, another Lit Hub piece explains how to make the ink that wrote Magna Carta, Hamlet, Pepys's Diary, the Declaration of Independence and Beethoven's Fifth. There's something lovely in the thought that a play, a symphony and a founding document were all, at bottom, set down in the same sort of dark liquid.

On the subject of history and fiction, France 24 has a Perspective piece in which the novelist Ian McGuire says that historical fiction is about filling in the gaps. I only have the headline to go on, so I can't tell you how he develops it, but it's a neat phrase, and one you might borrow for a class on why novels can teach what the archive cannot. For a different kind of history-haunted storytelling, the podcast Backlisted has rebroadcast its twenty-seventeen episode on Alan Garner's Red Shift, his fifth novel. Erica Wagner and S.F. Said discuss its layered storytelling, and the conversation also touches on Alan Partridge's Nomad, which is a pleasing detour.

Now to new novels, and the voices that carry them. The Guardian reviews Michael, Bob Mortimer's fourth novel. It follows a troubled teenager in nineteen-seventies Middlesbrough, and is framed by a narrator who is near death and is offered a strange choice. The reviewer praises its off-kilter charm and its warm, quirky voice. The Guardian also reviews The Brightness, Chad Harbach's sequel to The Art of Fielding. It's set fifteen years on at the fictional Westish college, and the reviewer finds it ambitious in its treatment of female agency, friendship and the messiness of early adulthood. And on BBC Radio 4's Open Book, Mary Beth Keane talks about Whale Harbour, her new family saga set in Ireland and the United States. She speaks about writing from family history, and says the book is partly for her father, who always wanted to see Montana. It runs to twelve minutes, so it's a tidy listen.

A handful of personal essays this morning are about reading and writing as lived experience. On Literary Hub, one piece considers Brian Blanchfield's novel Proxies and the respite of queer stories. It begins with a friend who handed over the book with a promise that the writer would love it, and it becomes a reflection on how fiction can console. Another is a lyrical essay, Song and Spirit, which begins with waking in a family home before dawn and works towards understanding a grandmother's deep devotion. It's intimate and atmospheric, with a strong sense of place and of character. A third will resonate with you as a teacher: a writer explains why she published her memoir under a pseudonym, partly because her students might read it. It raises interesting questions about voice, identity and the public self a teacher carries into the classroom.

And one more from Literary Hub that links poetry and painting: an essay imagining what William Blake would have made of artificial intelligence. It starts from the way the word icon has travelled from sacred image to double-clickable thumbnail, which is a surprisingly Blakean place to begin.

Finally, a bit of news from the prize world. Literary Hub introduces the finalists for the seventy-seventh National Book Awards, across fiction, poetry, nonfiction, translation and young people's literature. The winners will be announced this week at a ceremony in New York City, so there's time to browse the lists before then.

That's the shelf for today, Yamuna, and I hope something on it finds its way to your bedside table.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle, bookish Tuesday on the literary pages: a novelist who started again, a pastoral romance, a mystery from the court of Louis the Fourteenth, and a handful of new novels with voices worth listening to.

Let me begin with Anita Brookner, who turns up twice in the last couple of days. The New York Times has reviewed Hermione Lee's new biography, Anita Brookner: Art and Life. According to the review, the book corrects some of the public perceptions of the novelist's private life. Brookner's reputation has often rested on a particular image of her, and it seems Lee's careful work loosens that image a little. The title is worth a moment too. Art and Life, side by side, suggests a biography interested in how the one fed the other, which is exactly the kind of question you might put to a class: how much of a narrator's voice belongs to the author, and how much has been invented to carry the story?

The second piece comes from Literary Hub, and it's a more intimate companion. It's an essay on how Brookner restarted her life at fifty-two, beginning again as a novelist while she was still teaching. I rather like that detail. We so often hear about writers as if they arrive fully formed and young, and here is someone who found her second act in midlife, with a job to keep up at the same time. For a teacher who spends her days with other people's sentences, it may be a quietly encouraging read. Taken together, the review and the essay give you the biography and the human story behind it, and you could happily read them one after the other.

From there, let's step a very long way back in time. Literary Hub has an appreciative essay on Longus's pastoral romance, Daphnis and Chloe. The essay points out that the story opens with a prayer: that the book will bring pleasure and comfort to lovers. I find that a lovely way to begin a book. There's no pretence of grand purpose, only the hope that it will be a kindness to the people who read it. The essay dwells on the lyrical, musical quality of the prose, and it's the sort of piece that sends you back to the original, or at least makes you want to read a few lines aloud to hear how they sound. If you ever want a text for pupils that shows how prose can behave like song, an essay like this is a good place to start the conversation.

Staying with the materials of writing, there's a charming piece on how to make the ink used to write Hamlet, the Declaration of Independence, and Beethoven's Fifth. It also mentions Magna Carta and Pepys's Diary. What I enjoy about this is the shift in perspective. We usually think about what was written, and rarely about what it was written with. The piece treats ink as a thread running through history, connecting a play, a political document, a diary and a symphony, which are all very different kinds of making. There's something moving in the thought that the same sort of dark liquid sat behind Shakespeare's lines and Beethoven's notes. It might even make a nice opening for a lesson, a physical object to hold the imagination before you turn to the text itself.

And on a related note of art and ideas, Literary Hub also offers an essay imagining what William Blake would have thought of artificial intelligence. It begins with the word icon, and how it has travelled from sacred image to something we double-click, a little thumbnail on a screen. That's a clever way in, and Blake is such a natural figure for the question, being both a poet and a painter, someone for whom image and word were never really separate. Whatever one thinks of the subject, it's a nice example of the link between visual art and poetry that you enjoy, and it might spark a good discussion with older pupils about what we mean by image, and by making.

Now to history, and the way stories fill the gaps that records leave behind. Literary Hub's This Week in Literary History column looks at the Man in the Iron Mask, who died in the Bastille. He was a prisoner arrested in sixteen sixty-nine, during the reign of Louis the Fourteenth, and his identity was never revealed. It's a mystery rooted in French history, and rather close to home for you. What's striking is that the absence of facts is precisely what has made the figure so durable. Nobody knows who he was, so everybody can imagine him. That's a perfect illustration of why novelists are drawn to the silences in the historical record.

That idea is put into words, almost exactly, by the novelist Ian McGuire in a Perspective piece on France 24. His argument, in the headline at least, is that historical fiction is about filling in the gaps. I should be honest that all I have of that piece is the headline, so I can't tell you more about how he develops the thought. But the sentence is a good one on its own, and it sits very neatly beside the Iron Mask. History tells us that a man was arrested and that he died. Fiction asks what that was like, and who he was, and what he thought in the dark. If you teach the novel as a way of learning about the past, it's a useful phrase to offer a class.

There's another history-haunted work on the audio side. The podcast Backlisted has rebroadcast an episode from twenty seventeen on Alan Garner's Red Shift, his fifth novel. Erica Wagner and S.F. Said are the guests, and the book is described as layered and haunted by history, with strong narrative voice. If you don't know Garner, this is a lovely way in, because the conversation takes the book's structure seriously, and that's often where the pleasure lies in a novel that moves across time. The episode also touches, rather unexpectedly, on Alan Partridge's Nomad, which I mention only because it made me smile to find the two side by side.

On the subject of family history, there's a twelve-minute conversation on BBC Radio 4's Open Book with Mary Beth Keane about her new family saga, Whale Harbour, which is set in Ireland and the United States. Keane talks about writing from her own family's history, and I was touched by one detail: the book is partly for her father, who always wanted to see Montana. That's the kind of reason for writing a novel that you don't often hear stated so simply. It's a short listen and would fit nicely into a coffee break.

Moving to the new novels, with their voices. The Guardian has reviewed Bob Mortimer's fourth novel, Michael. It follows a troubled teenager in nineteen-seventies Middlesbrough, and the story is framed by a narrator who is near death and is offered a strange choice. The reviewer praises its off-kilter charm and its warm, quirky voice. I like the shape of it: a narrator at the end of life looking back on a boy in a particular place and time, with a curious choice hanging over everything. A frame like that always raises good questions about who is telling the story, and why, and what they might wish to change. It sounds like a book that wears its humanity lightly.

The Guardian also reviews Chad Harbach's The Brightness, a sequel to The Art of Fielding. It's set fifteen years on, at the fictional Westish college. The reviewer calls it ambitious, particularly in its attention to female agency, to friendship, and to the messiness of early adulthood. I think the interest of returning to an established place after a long gap is that a novelist can look at the same setting with different eyes, and it sounds as though Harbach has done just that, shifting the focus onto characters who have more to say this time. If you read the first book, it may be a satisfying return, and if you didn't, the review at least suggests the themes are accessible ones.

Now, a few personal essays that I think you may enjoy, since they're about reading and about language. The first, on Literary Hub, is about Brian Blanchfield's novel Proxies, and about the respite of queer stories. It begins with a friend who handed over the book with a promise that the writer would love it. It's a very human way into a piece about what fiction can do for us, which is to console, to recognise, and to offer shelter. Anyone who has pressed a book into a friend's hands will know that feeling of confident hope.

The second is a lyrical personal essay called Song and Spirit, about waking in a family home before dawn and coming to understand a grandmother's deep devotion. It's described as intimate and atmospheric, with a strong sense of place and a vivid character at the centre. Those are the qualities that make a short piece of non-fiction feel like a story, and it could be a lovely model for older pupils writing about a person or a place, where the early-morning light and the sounds of the house do much of the work.

The third raises a question that may land a little closer to home. A writer explains why she had to publish her memoir under a pseudonym, partly because her students might read it. It's an essay about identity and voice, and about the teacher's public self, the person who stands at the front of a classroom and the person who writes, and how the two might not always want to meet. I'd be curious what you make of it. It doesn't tell us, in the summary at least, how she resolved the tension, but the question itself is an interesting one for anyone who teaches and also loves to write.

Finally, a word on prizes. Literary Hub, on the sixteenth of November, introduced the finalists for the seventy-seventh National Book Awards, across fiction, poetry, nonfiction, translation and young people's literature. The winners are due to be announced this week at a ceremony in New York City. I don't have the names to hand, but the piece is there if you want to browse the shortlists, and it's always pleasant to see poetry and translation given a place beside the novels. It may be worth a look for some reading ideas, especially in the translation category.

So that's the morning: Brookner's second beginning, a pastoral prayer for lovers, the ink behind Hamlet and Beethoven, a masked prisoner nobody could name, and a few warm new voices to keep you company.

Enjoy the reading, Yamuna, and I hope the light over Belledonne is kind to you today.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Tuesday the seventeenth of November, and the next few weeks around you are full of theatre, music and small local happenings, with a few good reasons to head out.

Let me start with the stage, because the MC2 in Grenoble has a busy run. On Thursday the nineteenth and Friday the twentieth of November, it hosts "L'Ange du foyer", a theatre piece by Emma Dante, a director whose work is often built around strong ensemble characters. The listing gives little more than that, but her name alone may be reason enough. On Thursday the nineteenth, the MC2 also has "Último helecho", a music show by Nina Laisné, François Chaignaud and Nadia Larcher. Again the listing is brief, but a pairing of voice and performance like this suggests something worth seeing.

A week later, on Thursday the twenty-sixth of November, also at the MC2, the jazz musician Anne Paceo performs "Atlantis". That's a good option for an evening of contemporary jazz close to home. Then, from the ninth to the eleventh of December, there's "Same Same", a family circus show by Phare Circus. It's aimed at families rather than an adult evening, but it's lively, and could be a treat if you have little ones to bring along.

Slightly further ahead, on Wednesday the sixteenth of December at eight in the evening, the Hexagone Scène nationale in Meylan presents "Point de bascule" by Le Gravillon, running one hour forty. It follows a researcher who is also a cyclist, and who is offered an Air France deal to offset his carbon emissions. There is one further date, so it's worth checking the theatre's listing if the evening doesn't suit.

Now to things happening very close in time. Tomorrow, Wednesday the eighteenth of November, Pontcharra holds a celebration for its sporting champions and its volunteers, as Le Dauphiné Libéré reports. The piece is short, but it's a warm bit of community life just down the valley from you. Also tomorrow, at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage, there's a family show called "Jardins enchantés", a ciné-concert, which means a film accompanied by live music. That suits your taste for storytelling and concerts, even if it's pitched at younger audiences.

And starting today, the tour of the new film "Lapied" begins, with stops at Pontcharra, Allevard and Valgelon-La Rochette in Savoie. Le Dauphiné Libéré gives few details, so I'd check the local listings for the exact screening times at each stop.

Over in Grenoble, Ici-Grenoble reports an invitation to the launch evening of the Gragenda 2027, with a magic show, a concert and workshops. The text gives no date, so do check the listing before planning anything.

Allevard has two small pleasures for you. First, there's a free temporary exhibition called "L'avant de l'après", open now and running until the thirty-first of October next year. The listing doesn't say what it's about, but with nearly a year to go, you can visit whenever it suits you. Second, ici.fr has a local history piece asking why Allevard-les-Bains, in Belledonne, once had as many as four cemeteries. The text is short, but it's just the sort of curious little story that a place can hold, and might even stir up an idea for a walk through the town.

Looking to the outdoors and the winter ahead, Le Dauphiné Libéré says ten new cycling loops are planned for the Grésivaudan, which the paper calls the "vallée aux 100 châteaux", between Belledonne and Chartreuse. They are due from 2027, and could open up some lovely new rides or walks. Closer to the present, Les 7 Laux has opened pre-sales for its 2026-2027 season ski passes online. No closing date is given, so if you plan to ski this winter, booking early seems wise.

If you enjoy a flea market, there's news from La Tour-du-Pin, reported on the sixteenth of November. The Sunday vide-greniers there drew a full house and will carry on through the winter. It does lie a little beyond your usual thirty kilometres, but it's a pleasant excuse for a Sunday drive if you fancy a hunt for old books or prints.

Finally, in Chambéry, Le Pays Gessien reports that the Migrant'scène programme is inviting people to change how they see migration, through live performance, debate screenings and exhibitions. The report is only a headline, so I don't have dates or venues, but it may reward a closer look if the subject interests you.

So, plenty to choose from, Yamuna. I hope something among them tempts you out of the house this week.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Tuesday the seventeenth of November, and the news from around Belledonne and the valley is mostly about autumn evenings: a few things happening right now, a good run of stage shows at the MC2, and some longer-term pleasures to keep in your diary.

Let me start with what's closest in time, because several things fall today and tomorrow. Today, the seventeenth, is the start of the tour of the new film Lapied, reported by Le Dauphiné Libéré. The tour stops at Pontcharra, Allevard and Valgelon-La Rochette, over in Savoie. The report is short, and I don't have the screening times or venues, nor the dates of each stop. If the film appeals, a quick look at the local cinema or town hall listings will tell you which evening it reaches Pontcharra or Allevard, both of which are comfortably close to home.

Tomorrow, Wednesday the eighteenth, Pontcharra is holding a celebration for its sporting champions and its volunteers, again according to Le Dauphiné Libéré. The piece is brief, so I can't tell you the hour or the exact place, but it's the sort of small civic gathering that says a good deal about a town. It's a pleasant reminder of how many people quietly keep village and valley life going, the association members, the coaches, the people who set out the chairs.

Also tomorrow, the eighteenth, at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage, there's a family show called Jardins enchantés. It's a ciné-concert, which means a film accompanied by live music. The listing is short and doesn't say who is playing or how long it runs. But I thought of you with this one, because the form itself is lovely. A story told in images, with musicians in the room making the sound as it happens, is a very particular kind of storytelling. Even though it's aimed at families, it could be a gentle, rather beautiful way to spend an early evening if you like the idea of narrative and live music together.

Now to the MC2 in Grenoble, which has a run of things in the coming weeks. The first is this week. On Thursday the nineteenth and Friday the twentieth of November, the MC2 presents L'Ange du foyer, a theatre piece by Emma Dante. Dante is a director whose work is often built around strong ensemble characters, so if you enjoy stage work where the people on stage feel vivid and fully drawn, her name is a good one to know. The listing gives no further detail about the piece, so I can't tell you what it's about or how it unfolds. But the title alone, which echoes that old Victorian phrase for the idealised domestic woman, is intriguing for someone who spends her days with English literature. I'll only say the echo is there. I wouldn't want to claim the piece is about it.

On Thursday the nineteenth, the same evening as the first night of the Dante, the MC2 also has Último helecho, a music show by Nina Laisné, François Chaignaud and Nadia Larcher. The listing is brief, but the pairing of a singer with performers who work across voice and movement suggests something that is more than a straightforward concert. It's a Thursday-only date, so if you're tempted, it's the one to plan around.

A week later, on Thursday the twenty-sixth of November, the MC2 hosts the jazz concert by Anne Paceo, performing Atlantis. That's a good option for an evening of contemporary jazz close to home, and a little further ahead, which makes it easy to plan for.

Then in December, from the ninth to the eleventh, the MC2 has Same Same, a family circus show by Phare Circus. It's more of a family outing than an adult evening out, but it's local and lively. If you have nieces, nephews or friends with young children, it could be a good one to suggest, and the three dates give some flexibility.

Slightly further out, and a little way along the valley, the Hexagone Scène nationale in Meylan has Point de bascule by Le Gravillon, on Wednesday the sixteenth of December at eight in the evening. It runs for one hour forty minutes. It follows a researcher who is also a cyclist, and who is offered an Air France deal to offset his carbon emissions. The listing also mentions one further date, though it doesn't say when. It sounds like a piece that wrestles with a real moral puzzle through a character, which is often where theatre is at its best. A man with a bicycle and a very awkward offer is a promising setup.

Turning to Allevard, there are two things there that might suit your taste for culture and for stories of place. First, there's a temporary exhibition called L'avant de l'après, which is open now and runs all the way until the thirty-first of October twenty twenty-seven. It's free. The listing doesn't say what the theme is, so I can't tell you more than the title, which suggests something about before and after, about a moment of change. But with nearly a year to go, it's the sort of thing you can fit in on any gentle weekend, perhaps combined with a walk or lunch in Allevard, without having to plan around a deadline.

The other Allevard item is a local history piece from ici.fr, asking why Allevard-les-Bains, in Belledonne, at one time had as many as four cemeteries. The text I have is brief, so I can't give you the answer. But it's a question that makes you curious at once, and I suspect you'd enjoy it. Small local history of that kind, the odd detail that opens onto a bigger story about a place and its people, is a little like the way a good novel teaches history, through particulars rather than dates. It might be worth reading before a visit to the exhibition, so that you walk through the town with a slightly different eye.

Now to Grenoble and Chambéry, where a couple of programmes are announced without full details. From Ici-Grenoble.org comes an invitation to the launch evening of Gragenda twenty twenty-seven in Grenoble. The evening promises a magic show, a concert and workshops. The text gives no date, so do check the listing before you go. I can only tell you the mix sounds playful and varied.

In Chambéry, a programme called Migrant'scène offers live performance, screenings followed by debates, and exhibitions, all aimed at changing how people look at migration. This comes from Le Pays Gessien. It's only a headline, so I don't have dates or venues. But a programme that mixes theatre, film and exhibition around a single theme could be thought-provoking, particularly for someone who teaches texts where displacement and belonging are so often at the heart of the story. It's worth keeping an eye out for the full details.

Let me finish with the outdoors, the markets and the winter, which are always a bit of a reward at this time of year.

First, some good news for walkers and cyclists. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that ten new cycling loops are planned for the Grésivaudan, the valley the paper calls the vallée aux cent châteaux, between Belledonne and Chartreuse. They are due from twenty twenty-seven. I don't have routes or distances, but it's a constructive piece of local news, and a rather lovely nickname for the valley you look down on every day. If you cycle, or have friends who do, it's something to look forward to in the spring and summer.

Then there's a flea market, though I should say it's a little beyond our usual radius. At La Tour-du-Pin, the Sunday vide-greniers has drawn a full house, reported on the sixteenth of November, and it will carry on through the winter. That's a good sign for anyone who likes browsing for old books, prints, odd bits of china and the occasional surprise. It's further than I would normally include, so it would be a proper day out rather than a quick detour. But if you're in the mood for a Sunday outing, and you don't mind some cold air, it's worth knowing there's a market that doesn't stop for the season.

And finally, a note for the winter ahead. At Les 7 Laux, pre-sales for the twenty twenty-six to twenty twenty-seven season ski pass are already open online. The page gives no closing date for the pre-sale, so if you're planning to ski this winter, it makes sense to book early rather than wait.

So that's the picture: a few things to catch this week, a good run of stage evenings at the MC2, and plenty of gentle ideas for the months ahead. Wrap up warm, and enjoy whichever of them tempts you.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet couple of days for official BFI news, but there's a good handful of pieces for your oral themes and for the 2027 texts, with a few pleasant surprises besides.

Let me start with the oral themes, where the dystopian and post-apocalyptic works are well served. London Now has an essay called "Rewriting the Past to Control the Present: The Haunting Prescience of 1984". Its argument is that Orwell seems almost prophetic about how history can be rewritten to serve power. That should suit you, since it treats the novel as a way of learning how history works, and it would give pupils a clear thesis to agree or argue with before an oral on 1984.

For Parable of the Sower, The Good Men Project has published an excerpt from a book called Science Fiction Ecologies, on how Octavia Butler used science fiction to think about ecological collapse. What I like is that it treats the novel as a thinking tool rather than a string of plot points. It could be good background reading for you, or for a stronger pupil who wants to go beyond summary.

Related to that, The Conversation looks at six post-apocalyptic novels and how differently each imagines the end of the world. The text I have gives no titles, so I can't say whether any are on our list. But the question of how different writers picture collapse is a natural framing for comparing The Road with Butler.

And Atwood's Gilead is in the news twice. ABC News has an item on The Testaments, the new screen story set in Gilead, described as a coming-of-age tale and featuring Chase Infiniti. Separately, Broadcast Dialogue reports that The Testaments was one of the leading winners at the 2026 DGC Awards, alongside Small Achievable Goals. Both pieces are really only headlines, and this is screen news rather than literature, so I'd treat them as a way of catching pupils' attention, since some will already know the series. The more interesting classroom question is how a story about young women growing up inside Gilead changes the way we look back at The Handmaid's Tale.

Now to the 2027 session, starting with Blake. Literary Hub has an essay asking what William Blake would have thought of artificial intelligence. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you where it lands. But Blake, with his suspicion of rigid systems and his sense of imagination as something living, feels like a natural fit for the question, and it could make a lively opening for a discussion on Songs of Innocence and of Experience. It may be worth reading before deciding whether to use it with pupils.

Hamlet is the busiest text this week. Binghamton University has a short piece asking why audiences keep returning to tragedies, from Hamlet to Faust. It's brief, but the question itself is a good one for seconde or première: why do we choose to watch suffering, and what do we get from it? It would work well as a spoken warm-up before anyone opens the play.

On the stage side, Love London Love Culture has a review round-up of a Hamlet at the Barbican, billed as "Hamlet Hail to the Thief". I only have the headline, so the critics' verdicts aren't visible to me, but a round-up like that is useful for comparing how different reviewers read the same production. In Greece, Ticketmaster announces a Hamlet at the Theatre of the NO, directed by Nicolas Zlatoff. There's no date in the text, and it's a long way from Les Adrets, so that one is more a curiosity than a plan. Still, it's a reminder of how widely the play is staged.

Looking ahead to the 2028 session, RTE reports that Dublin's Gate Theatre has launched its 2027 season, and the headline links David Ireland with A Raisin in the Sun. The text is thin, so I can't tell you who is directing or when it plays, but it's encouraging to see Hansberry's play in a major season. It's worth keeping an eye on for production details, which can make good material for a unit later on.

Next, a few pieces about storytelling and place, which I suspect you'll enjoy. Pacific Media Network profiles Jesse Tima, a storyteller who has taken his Pacific act to Shakespeare's Globe in London. Oral storytelling reaching one of the great stages seems a fitting thing to mention in the same breath as Under Milk Wood, though that's my connection rather than the article's. In the California Review of Books, John Freeman takes a journey through the Golden State's newer literature, under the title "California Rewritten". I only have the headline and byline, so I don't know which writers he covers, but it sounds like fiction tied closely to place. And in Newry, an actor is backing the name of Sean Hollywood for a new theatre. The text is short, but it's a small, warm story about a community naming a stage after one of its own.

Two last things. TED-Ed has a video of cognitive scientist Tania Lombrozo, recorded at TEDxNewEngland in October 2025, explaining why more information can actually make learning harder. It isn't about literature, but it could be a good starter for seconde or première, especially before tackling something dense like Hamlet or Dickens. And for pure lightness, The Sunday Guardian asks when the new Pride and Prejudice adaptation with Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden will reach streaming. There's no release date given, and Pride and Prejudice isn't on our programme, though Emma is among the oral themes, so Austen may still be in the air.

That's the corner for today, and I hope the Blake essay turns out to be as intriguing as its title.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Tuesday in mid-November, and today's corner has a pleasant spread of dystopias, Hamlet in three cities, a couple of programme texts in unexpected company, and a small gift of a classroom starter at the end.

Let me begin with the oral themes, because several items cluster there. The strongest of them is an essay from London Now called "Rewriting the Past to Control the Present: The Haunting Prescience of 1984". As the title suggests, it argues that Orwell seems almost prophetic about how power works by rewriting history. I think this one is worth your time, for two reasons. First, it is directly useful for the oral theme on 1984. Second, its central argument is exactly the sort of thing you like: a novel that teaches how history gets made and unmade, rather than merely what happened. If you have première students who find Orwell a little too familiar, a little too much like a poster on a bedroom wall, an essay that puts the Ministry of Truth's habits at the centre of the discussion could make the book feel urgent again. You might ask them to find a single sentence in the novel where the past is altered quietly, and then to say why the quietness is more frightening than the violence.

Alongside that, The Good Men Project has published an excerpt from a book on how Octavia Butler used science fiction to think about ecological collapse. This is useful background for Parable of the Sower, which is on the oral list. What appeals to me is the way the excerpt treats the novel as a thinking tool rather than a sequence of plot points. That is a very good habit to pass on to students, who often retell the story when you ask them to analyse it. Used well, a text like this could help a candidate say what the book is doing, not just what happens in it. It may be a little dense for seconde, but for première or terminale, or simply for your own preparation, it looks promising.

Related to that, The Conversation has a piece looking at six post-apocalyptic novels and how differently each of them imagines the end of the world. I should be honest that the text I have doesn't name the six books, so I can't tell you whether The Road or Parable of the Sower is among them. But the premise is a good one for teaching. Cormac McCarthy and Octavia Butler both give us collapse, and yet the two books feel almost opposite in temperament: one stripped down to ash and a father and son, the other looking for a way of building something afterwards. A comparison of how each imagines the end, and what each thinks survives, would make a good oral-preparation exercise. If the article turns out to name other titles, so much the better, as it could supply comparison points.

Now to Gilead. There are two items this time, and both are thin, so I will be brief. ABC News carries a piece on The Testaments, described as a new coming-of-age story set in Gilead, with Chase Infiniti among the cast. And Broadcast Dialogue reports that The Testaments and a title called Small Achievable Goals were the leading winners at the 2026 DGC Awards. In both cases I only have the headline, so I cannot tell you anything about the quality of the work. What I can say is that The Testaments is Atwood's sequel to The Handmaid's Tale, which is on the oral list, and that students are often curious about what happens beyond the first book. It is, at the very least, a good reason for some of them to be asking questions about Gilead this week. A coming-of-age story in that world is also an interesting angle: the original novel is so much about one woman's interior voice, and it would be a fine exercise to ask how a younger narrator might change the way the world is seen. I would treat these as conversation starters rather than resources.

That brings me to Hamlet, which turns up three times today, and is a fixture of the 2027 session.

The first is academic. Binghamton University has an article asking why audiences keep returning to tragedies such as Hamlet and Faust, under the title "humans find tragedies irresistible". The text I have is brief, so I can't say what answer it gives, but the question itself is a good opener for seconde or première. Why would anyone choose to sit through a story that ends badly? Students usually have strong, and often surprising, opinions on this, and the question leads naturally into Hamlet's delay, the ghost, the play within the play, and the odd pleasure of watching someone think himself into a corner. You could ask them to defend the idea that we go to tragedy for comfort rather than for pain, and see where they land.

The second is a London production. Love London Love Culture has a review round-up for a Hamlet at the Barbican, and the headline gives the title as Hamlet Hail to the Thief. Again, only the headline came through, so I cannot tell you what the critics thought. But a review round-up is a lovely classroom object in itself. Several critics responding to the same staging, sometimes disagreeing sharply, is a ready-made lesson in how interpretation works. If you can open the page, you might choose two reviews that differ, and ask students which one persuades them, and why. That is a quiet way of teaching close reading and argument, with Shakespeare as the subject.

The third is further afield. Ticketmaster Greece announces a production of Hamlet at the Theatre of the NO, directed by Nicolas Zlatoff. There's no date in the text I have, and the venue is in Greece, so this is not something to plan a trip around. But it is a small reminder that the play is being staged all over Europe, which might interest students who like to think of Shakespeare as a living, travelling text rather than a school set book. If any of your pupils have family connections to Greece, it might even be a point of contact.

Moving on to other programme texts, two items touch the 2027 and 2028 sessions.

Literary Hub has an essay asking what William Blake would have thought of artificial intelligence. Songs of Innocence and of Experience is on the 2027 programme, and this may be a fresh way in. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what the author argues. But Blake is a natural candidate for the question: a poet and engraver who distrusted cold systems and mechanical thinking, and who made his own books by hand. Even without having read the essay, I can imagine students enjoying the thought experiment. You could ask them to choose one poem, perhaps a pair like the two Chimney Sweepers, or The Lamb and The Tyger, and write a short reaction as if Blake were looking at a chatbot. It is playful, but it forces them back to the poems to justify what they say.

And from Dublin, RTE reports that the Gate Theatre has launched its 2027 season, with David Ireland and A Raisin in the Sun named in the headline. A Raisin in the Sun is on the 2028 list. The text is thin, so I cannot say who is directing, who is in the cast, or what the dates are, and I would not want to guess. But it is encouraging to see Hansberry's play in the season of a major theatre. If you are already thinking ahead to 2028, it is worth keeping an eye on the Gate's announcements for details.

A few items belong less to the syllabus than to the wider world of stories and the people who tell them.

Pacific Media Network profiles Jesse Tima, a storyteller who has taken his Pacific act to Shakespeare's Globe in London. The piece begins with making up stories and ends at one of the most famous stages in the English-speaking world, and I like that arc. It is a story about oral storytelling reaching a major theatre, and it might be a nice thing to show to students who think of Shakespeare as something that belongs only to written English. The Globe was built for voices, after all. It could connect with your interest in narrators and in stories you can step into without needing to know the culture first.

On a similar note of place and voice, the California Review of Books has a feature by John Freeman called "California Rewritten: A Journey Through the Golden State's New Literature". I only have the headline and the byline, so I can't say which writers are covered. But John Freeman is a name many readers of contemporary fiction will know, and a tour of newer literature rooted in one place is the sort of thing you tend to enjoy. It is not a BFI item in a strict sense, but it might feed your own reading or suggest a regional approach to a unit.

Closer to home, though not very close, Newry.ie reports that a Newry actor is backing the name of Sean Hollywood for a new theatre. The text is short, so there is little more to say, but it is a pleasant little local arts story about a theatre being named after a person from the community. If you ever wanted a way into the Irish texts on the programme, such as Dancing at Lughnasa, a story about how a town remembers its own people might be a modest starting point.

One item stands apart, and I will mention it only briefly. The Sunday Guardian asks when a new Pride and Prejudice adaptation, starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden, will reach streaming. There's no release date in the text, so it is really a streaming notice. Pride and Prejudice is not on the programme, though Emma is on the oral list, so it is only of passing interest. If your students are Austen readers, it may be a pleasant thing to bring up in conversation, and a chance to ask what an adaptation has to change in order to stay faithful.

Finally, there is something for the start of a lesson. TED-Ed has put out a video from TEDxNewEngland, recorded in October 2025, in which the cognitive scientist Tania Lombrozo explains why more information can sometimes make learning harder. It is general learning science rather than literature, but I think it could be a good starter for seconde or première. Students are often convinced that the way to master a difficult text is to gather more and more commentary and notes. A short talk that questions that assumption might persuade them to try reading more slowly, and to sit with a single passage of Blake or Shakespeare before reaching for a study guide. I would suggest watching it yourself first, to see whether the register and length suit your classes.

So, in short: the 1984 essay and the Butler excerpt look the most substantial, Hamlet is getting plenty of attention across Europe, and a number of the other items are only headlines, so I would treat them as prompts rather than sources until you have had a look.

Enjoy the day, Yamuna, and may your students find something irresistible in the tragedies.

Good morning, Yamuna. I've gathered a handful of small, bright stories from the last two days, some musical, some medical, and a good few with feathers, fur or wheat in them.

Let me start with one that feels made for you. Upworthy tells of a man who wanted to see music. After three years of experiments, he paired a piano with bioluminescent algae, so that each note is answered by light. The write-up is short, but it describes the result as magical to watch, and it's a lovely meeting of music, science and nature. Upworthy also has a gentler musical treat: a 1973 unplugged medley in which the Bee Gees pay tribute to the Beatles. It is described as gorgeous, and it has that stripped-back, live quality you tend to enjoy. And from franceinfo, a film note: Ulya, directed by Viesturs Kairiss, a coming-of-age tale with striking photography, loosely inspired by a legendary Latvian basketball player. It has been chosen to represent Latvia at the 2027 Oscars, and it avoids the usual biopic conventions.

Now, some human stories, the kind that would make a good opening paragraph. Good News Network follows David, an English teenager who in 1994 was on holiday on the Greek island of Kos, where a group of children formed a close circle. One of them, Jodie, became his wife thirty-two years later. It is a warm, character-led story, and a gentle reminder that some plots take a very long time to resolve.

In a similar spirit, Upworthy reports on Maren and David Douglass, who saw a middle schooler waiting dangerously close to traffic at a bus stop. They built a cosy reading nook there. It's a small thing, but a very concrete kindness. And Reasons to be Cheerful visits Against Da Grain, a barbershop on Staten Island's North Shore, to ask whether the trust built between barbers and their customers might help improve health among Black men. It's about everyday places quietly doing useful work.

On health, two items with real substance. The Optimist Daily revisits a wrist device for people with Tourette's. In a 2023 University of Nottingham trial of one hundred and twenty-one people in the UK, the prototype, called Neupulse, reduced tic frequency by an average of twenty-five percent. The piece looks at how users describe it three years on. A quarter fewer tics is a practical, tangible gain.

The other is from Good News Network. Doctors at Franciscan Health, a Catholic health system in the American Midwest, report what they describe as the first bone marrow transplant used to treat a non-malignant disease. The donor marrow came from a deceased organ donor, and the patient was a forty-year-old woman with aplastic anaemia. It's a real medical advance with very human stakes.

Then to the natural world, where several stories turn on rescue and revival. Upworthy looks back six years after beavers were brought to a desert region to help save a dying river, and reports that the results are in. The piece is brief, but it is a genuinely hopeful story about restoration that works.

From the plains of Parma, Good News Network tells of a farmer, Claudio Grossi, who found shrivelled, unknown seeds in his attic, and, to his surprise, grew an ancient wheat from them, a so-called miracle grain. It reads like a small parable, and it has implications for the diversity of what we eat.

Also from Good News Network, and also in Greece: climbers found an orphaned seal pup on a beach at the foot of a cliff and carried it back up to safety. The species is critically endangered in Greece, so this small rescue matters. Staying on the Greek coast, The Optimist Daily describes a cleanup on the islet of Patroklos in the Saronic Gulf. Volunteers logged what they found, including a beer can from the 1990s World Cup, and the data became a pollution map. It's a clever bit of civic science with a memorable hook.

Further afield, Good News Network reports that Airbnb's chief executive, Brian Chesky, has given one hundred million dollars to San Francisco's parks. The gift was announced with Mayor Daniel Lurie in Golden Gate Park, and it is the largest single-donor gift in the city's history.

Finally, two items closer to home in spirit, if not quite in geography. From Le Dauphiné Libéré, the town of Pontcharra will celebrate its sporting champions and its volunteers on the eighteenth of November, tomorrow. The note is short, but it's a good piece of local community life, just down the valley from Les Adrets.

And from franceinfo, something to make you smile with your coffee. Organisers have chosen Seraffine, a cow from the Auvergne with a lovely powdery red coat, as the face of the 2027 Salon international de l'agriculture. She follows a difficult 2025, when no cattle were shown because of the nodular dermatosis health crisis, so her return is a cheerful sign.

That's your lot for today, and I hope at least one of these stays with you on the walk down to the valley.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news arrives in a few loose families: music and light, small stories about people, healing of various kinds, and a handful of tender things done for animals, land and neighbours.

Let me begin with something that feels made for you, because it sits where music, science and a touch of poetry meet. Upworthy tells of a man who wanted to "see music". He spent three years experimenting, and the result is a piano paired with bioluminescent algae, so that the sound becomes light. The write-up is short, but it describes the effect as magical to watch, and I can well believe it. Bioluminescent algae glow when they are disturbed, and so you can imagine each note leaving a faint trace of blue in the dark, as though the music had a visible breath. It is the sort of image one could set a class loose on. What would a Romantic poet have made of it? Or a synaesthete narrator? There is a short story waiting inside that piano.

Staying with music, Upworthy also resurfaces a lovely piece of archive: in 1973 the Bee Gees sang an unplugged medley as a tribute to the Beatles. Upworthy calls it gorgeous. It is the kind of thing worth ten minutes with a cup of tea, because stripped-back harmony shows how much a song carries before any production is added. Three voices, a tribute, and nothing to hide behind.

And a little further into the world of storytelling, franceinfo recommends "Ulya", a coming-of-age tale directed by Viesturs Kairiss. It is loosely inspired by the life of a legendary Latvian basketball player. What franceinfo praises is its striking photography, and the fact that it avoids the usual conventions of the biopic. The film has been chosen to represent Latvia at the 2027 Oscars. I mention it not for the awards but for the idea: a life retold as an initiation story rather than a list of achievements, and with a visual eye that sounds worth seeing.

Now to people, and one story that reads almost like a novel. Good News Network brings us a pair of pen pals. In 1994 David, an English teenager, was on holiday on the Greek island of Kos, where a group of children formed a close circle, the way children do on holiday, quickly and completely. One of them was Jodie. The letters, the friendship across distance, and then, thirty-two years later, Jodie has become his wife. There is something so satisfying in the shape of it. A summer on a Greek island, a correspondence kept alive on paper, and an ending that took more than three decades to arrive. If you ever want an example for your pupils of a story with a long, patient narrative arc, this one has it, and it happens to be true.

A smaller, kinder tale of people comes from Upworthy. Maren and David Douglass, homeowners, noticed a middle schooler waiting for the bus far too close to the traffic. Instead of simply worrying about it, they built a cosy reading nook at the bus stop. A safer place to wait, and a book-friendly one at that. The piece is brief, but I like how concrete it is: they saw a problem, and they answered it with carpentry and a bit of warmth.

There is a similar spirit in a feature from Reasons to be Cheerful, about a barbershop called Against Da Grain on the North Shore of Staten Island. The question is whether the trust that builds up between barbers and their customers can be turned into better health for Black men. A barbershop is a place where people talk, where they return regularly, and where they are known by name, and the feature looks at how that everyday trust might do useful work in people's health. It is a good reminder that care does not always happen in clinics; sometimes it happens in a chair, over a conversation.

Then a gift on a very large scale, from Good News Network. The Airbnb chief executive, Brian Chesky, has given one hundred million dollars to San Francisco's parks. It was announced alongside Mayor Daniel Lurie in Golden Gate Park, and it is the largest single-donor gift in the city's history. The report is brief, so I can't tell you more about how the money will be spent, but a gift to public parks is a gift to everyone, whether they walk, read on a bench, or simply cross through on the way to somewhere else.

Let me turn to health, where there are two items with real human stakes.

The first comes from Good News Network, and concerns a medical first. Doctors at Franciscan Health, a Catholic health system in the American Midwest, report what they describe as the first bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease. The donor marrow came from a deceased organ donor, and the patient was a forty-year-old woman with aplastic anaemia. Aplastic anaemia is a condition in which the body stops making enough blood cells, so it matters a great deal that there may be another route to treatment. I would add the careful note that this is the doctors' own description of it as a first, and it concerns one patient. But it opens a door, and behind it is a person whose life may now look different.

The second is from The Optimist Daily, and it is about Tourette's. In 2023, a trial run by the University of Nottingham in the United Kingdom, with one hundred and twenty-one people, tested a prototype wrist device called Neupulse. On average it reduced the frequency of tics by twenty-five percent. Now, three years on, The Optimist Daily reports on how users describe living with it. A quarter fewer tics may sound modest in a headline, but for someone living with Tourette's, it can mean a calmer afternoon, a quieter lesson, an easier conversation. And I like that this is a follow-up: not just the trial result, but what happens afterwards, in ordinary lives.

Now to nature, where several stories this week point the same way: that patient, practical effort can restore things.

Upworthy looks back at a project in which beavers were brought to a desert region to try to save a dying river. Six years on, the results are in, and the story is told as one of restoration that works. The piece is brief, and I won't pretend to give you figures that it doesn't, but the shape of it is wonderful: a creature famous for building, put to work on a landscape that needed repair. It is a quiet argument that we sometimes don't need to invent solutions when nature already has a skilled engineer on call.

From Italy, Good News Network offers what it nearly calls a parable. On the plains of Parma, a farmer named Claudio Grossi found some unknown, shrivelled seeds in his attic. He planted them, and, unexpectedly, they grew into an ancient wheat, the sort of grain described as a "miracle". It is a warm story of an unlikely revival, and it has a serious side too, because the survival of old grains matters for the diversity of what we eat. I find it very literary, honestly: the forgotten thing in the attic, the seeds that seemed finished and were not. One could build a whole novel on that premise, with the farm, the family, the past quietly waiting upstairs.

Greece provides two stories, one for animals and one for the coast. First, the rescue. Good News Network reports that climbers in Greece found an orphaned seal pup on a beach at the foot of a cliff, and carried it back up to safety. The species is critically endangered in Greece, so this was not a trivial kindness; a single pup matters. There is something moving in the picture of climbers, whose whole purpose that day was to go up, turning their strength and their skill to the carrying of a small animal.

Second, from The Optimist Daily, a coastline cleanup on Patroklos, an islet in the Saronic Gulf. The volunteers did not just collect litter; they logged it, item by item, and turned the record into a pollution map. Among the things found was a beer can from the 1990s World Cup, which is a rather marvellous detail, a little time capsule of rubbish. It makes the point that litter is not just mess but evidence, and that careful counting can turn a clean-up into a piece of civic science that tells us where the problem comes from and how long it has lasted.

And to finish, a pair of items closer to home, in spirit and in geography.

From franceinfo, something light and cheerful about French rural life. Organisers have chosen Seraffine, a cow from the Auvergne with, in their words, a pretty powdered red dress, as the face of the 2027 Salon international de l'agriculture. She returns to the spotlight after 2025, when no cattle were shown at all because of the nodular dermatosis health crisis. So there is a small note of recovery in her selection: the cattle are back, and she is their ambassador. If you are fond of producers' markets, you may enjoy imagining her presiding over the whole affair.

And a very local note from Le Dauphiné Libéré. Tomorrow, the eighteenth of November, the town of Pontcharra will hold a celebration for its sporting champions and its volunteers. The announcement is brief, but it is a lovely reminder of how much of a community runs on people who give their time without being asked, and who are, for one evening, thanked in public. And it is just down the valley from you in the Grésivaudan.

So, a piano that turns notes into light, a wheat that came back from an attic, a seal carried up a cliff, and a town thanking its volunteers; I hope one of them keeps you company through the day.

Given how much you enjoy a well-built thriller, you might find it gripping, if you are in the mood for something serious.

Good morning, Yamuna. This is a rich couple of days for you, with a lot from ARTE on painting and history, some lovely opera and ballet to dip into, and a pair of thrillers that are getting people talking.

Let me begin with ARTE, where the documentaries lean towards art and history. The one I'd put first is a film on Paul Cézanne, "pionnier de l'art moderne", made by Grit Lederer in twenty twenty-five and running fifty-three minutes. It follows his work back to Aix-en-Provence and to the family bastide, the Jas de Bouffan, where he experimented before becoming one of the founders of modern art. It's available on ARTE until the twenty-second of December, so there's no rush, but it's the kind of film that sits very happily alongside a novel. Next comes "Byzance, la plus grande coloc du monde ?", a ninety-minute film by Jacques Plaisant from this year. It traces the Byzantine Empire from three hundred and thirty to fourteen fifty-three through its archaeological treasures, from Istanbul all the way to the Louvre. It's history told through objects, which I think suits you well.

Also on ARTE is "L'Iran raconté par ses femmes", on the era of the last shah, which you can watch in full on the ARTE website. It's told through personal testimony, so the history comes through lived voices rather than a lecture, much as a good narrator would give it to you. And there's a lighter, more contemporary piece in the Twist strand called "Princesses : la fin du rêve". It looks at young women who want to be treated like princesses, taking in debutante auditions in Dresden, the influence of Disney, and whether feminist rap might change the picture. It could spark a few ideas about fairy tales and how they get handed down.

Now to music and the stage. The Royal Ballet and Opera has put several things on its YouTube channel. The most passionate is the Act One love duet from Puccini's Tosca, "Qual'occhio al mondo", sung by Freddie De Tommaso as Cavaradossi and Anna Netrebko as Tosca, filmed at the Royal Opera House. It's a short excerpt, and a lovely thing to play with a coffee.

From the same channel there's a film of Jette Parker Artists talking about performing Bizet's Carmen, in Damiano Michieletto's Spanish-set staging. The nice link for you is that the opera comes from Prosper Mérimée's novella, so it could make a neat pairing with the written text if you ever wanted to show the two side by side in class.

And for something more visual, there's a behind-the-scenes video on the costumes for Kenneth MacMillan's ballet Manon, designed by Nicholas Georgiadis. It shows how the fabric and the detail follow Manon's fall, from Parisian high society to hardship. It's a rather literary way of looking at costume, since the clothes are telling the story as much as the dancing is. It's also on YouTube.

Beyond the screen, The Guardian has a handful of reviews and one piece of news that might interest you. The first is about something coming in February. Rambert is staging a dance version of Russell T Davies's series "It's a Sin", about a group of gay friends in London in the nineteen-eighties during the Aids crisis. It opens at Aviva Studios in Manchester, and a trailer is already out. The piece puts the dancefloor at its heart, and the freedom of clubbing, which seems a moving way to approach that story.

On the listening side, The Guardian reviews Anna Lapwood's album "Not All Those Who Wander Are Lost". She turns Howard Shore's Lord of the Rings score into a thirty-eight-minute organ symphony, with the Nidaros Cathedral Girls' Choir, and it tells the story in chronological order. It sounds like a beautiful thing to put on of an evening.

There are two more reviews from the opera world. One is of Mid Wales Opera's touring Gianni Schicchi, Puccini's comic opera, at Theatr Brycheiniog in Brecon. The production leans into commedia dell'arte, and the reviewer enjoyed its fraud, fun and farce. The other is of "Spark", a new family opera by Lucy Armstrong, performed by Glyndebourne Youth Opera at Glyndebourne. It's about grief and loss, set in a secret world above the rooftops, and the reviewer praises its lightness of touch and the young performers.

Now to the thrillers, though I have to be honest that the details are thin. Wales Online reports that a Netflix thriller series is keeping viewers up until three in the morning, but all we have is the headline, so I can't tell you the title or the plot. Separately, MovieWeb says a six-episode Harlan Coben thriller reached number one on the streaming charts within four days of release. Again the item gives no platform, only the headline. Still, Coben is a reliable name for twisty, gripping plots, so it's worth checking what's new on Netflix when you next look.

One dance item to mention, with a caveat. Coverage is out on when fans can see "The Symphony of Dance", a documentary by Derek Hough and Hayley Erbert Hough. It's squarely your sort of subject, but it streams on Hulu rather than any of your platforms, and the report says very little, so I'd simply keep an eye out for it.

Lastly, The Guardian is launching a twice-weekly culture videocast, hosted by Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko, starting this Thursday, the nineteenth of November. Thursdays bring a fresh take on a big cultural moment, and on Sundays each host introduces the other to a favourite series, book or album, which might turn up some good recommendations.

That's the lot, Yamuna, so I hope you find a quiet hour tonight for Cézanne.
