Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Tuesday. Here is your Daily Yam for the seventeenth of November.

Let's begin with painting, and with how much a canvas can hold. The National Gallery has a video on how Jan van Eyck made portraiture new in the fifteenth century. Curators from London and Bruges talk about his realism and the hidden visual clues tucked into his work. Then there is a piece in The Guardian on a new biography of Edward Hopper. It suggests that his marriage to Josephine Nivison Hopper, and the troubles in their bedroom, may have seeped into his famous, melancholy paintings. The article asks how far a painter's private life can be read into his canvases, a question you could happily set a class. And closer to home, L'Impartial de la Drôme has a piece on a painting from Romans-sur-Isère that stands as a witness to a vanished Isère, local history and art meeting in a single frame.

On to the written word. Literary Hub has an article on how the ink was made that wrote Magna Carta, Hamlet, Pepys's Diary, the Declaration of Independence and Beethoven's Fifth. It's a lovely reminder that great words and great music began as something physical, mixed and brewed by hand. Then the Backlisted podcast is rebroadcasting a 2017 episode on Alan Garner's Red Shift, his fifth novel. Erica Wagner and S.F. Said discuss its layered, history-haunted storytelling, and the conversation also wanders to Alan Partridge's Nomad. And on France 24, in its Perspective series, the novelist Ian McGuire says that historical fiction is about filling in the gaps the record leaves. I only have the headline, but it is a phrase worth carrying around all day.

Now your BFI corner. London Now has an essay on how Orwell's 1984 seems so prophetic about rewriting the past to control the present. Its argument about history and power should be a strong resource for the oral theme on 1984. And for Parable of the Sower, The Good Men Project has published a book excerpt on how Octavia Butler used science fiction to think about ecological collapse. It treats the novel as a thinking tool rather than a string of plot points, which makes it useful background reading.

Time for some good news, and two small marvels. Upworthy tells of a man who wanted to see music. After three years of experiments, he paired a piano with bioluminescent algae, so that the notes appear as light. The text is short, but it is described as magical to watch, and I can well believe it. And from the plains of Parma, Good News Network brings us the farmer Claudio Grossi, who found shrivelled seeds in his attic and, rather unexpectedly, grew an ancient wheat from them. It is a warm story of an unlikely revival, with implications for food diversity, and it reads rather like a small parable.

If you fancy an evening in front of the screen, ARTE has a ninety-minute documentary by Jacques Plaisant, Byzance, mille ans qui ont changé le monde, made in France in twenty twenty-six. It follows the Byzantine Empire from the year three hundred and thirty to fourteen fifty-three through its archaeological treasures, from Istanbul to the Louvre. For something more passionate, the Royal Ballet and Opera has put on YouTube Freddie De Tommaso as Cavaradossi and Anna Netrebko as Tosca, singing the Act One love duet, Qual'occhio al mondo, from Puccini's Tosca at the Royal Opera House.

A word from the French pages. Franceinfo reviews Ulya, directed by Viesturs Kairiss, a coming-of-age tale with striking photography, loosely inspired by the life of a legendary Latvian basketball player. It has been chosen to represent Latvia at the twenty twenty-seven Oscars, and it avoids the usual biopic conventions. And for the language lover, The Local France explains the expression être à la masse, to be a bit out of it, which may come from electrical wiring. It's a short piece, but I always enjoy learning where an idiom was born.

Finally, a couple of things close to home. In Allevard, there is a free temporary exhibition called L'avant de l'après, open until the thirty-first of October twenty twenty-seven. The listing gives no detail about its theme, but with that long a run you can go whenever the mood takes you. And ici.fr asks a rather intriguing question about Allevard-les-Bains, in Belledonne: why did the commune at one time have as many as four cemeteries? The piece is brief, but it is just the kind of small local history that sends one off down a side path.

That is everything for this morning. I hope your Tuesday is full of good words, good light and a little bit of wonder, Yamuna.
